q-8078:
To write $z$ in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3\sqrt{3})^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36}=6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3}{3\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=6$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=6\,{\text{e}}^{\pi \text{i}/6}.
$$

q-17518:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2}{-1})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-2)| \\  & ≈2.034.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{5}$ and $\theta =2.034$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=\sqrt{5}\,{\text{e}}^{2.034\,\text{i}}\,.
$$

q-46507:
First, let's factor out $-4$ from the expression. We have

$$
-100-36{m}^{2}=-4(25+9{m}^{2}).
$$

Let's now focus on factoring the expression $(25+9{m}^{2}).$

To factor a sum of squares, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}25+9{m}^{2} & =25-(-9{m}^{2}) \\  & =25-(9{\text{i}}^{2}{m}^{2}) \\  & ={5}^{2}-{(3\text{i}m)}^{2} \\  & =(5+3\text{i}m)(5-3\text{i}m)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into the expression, we get

$$
-4(25+9{m}^{2})=-4(5+3\text{i}m)(5-3\text{i}m).
$$

q-170502:
First, let's factor the expression as a perfect square trinomial in ${w}^{2}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{4}+36{w}^{2}+81 & ={(2{w}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot (2{w}^{2})\cdot 9+{9}^{2} \\  & =(2{w}^{2}+9)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to factor the sum of squares in the parentheses. To do this, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{w}^{2}+9 & =2{w}^{2}-(-9) \\  & =2{w}^{2}-(9{\text{i}}^{2}) \\  & =(\sqrt{2}w)^{2}-(3\text{i})^{2} \\  & =(\sqrt{2}w+3\text{i})(\sqrt{2}w-3\text{i})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{4}+36{w}^{2}+81 & =(2{w}^{2}+9)^{2} \\  & =((\sqrt{2}w+3\text{i})(\sqrt{2}w-3\text{i}))^{2} \\  & =(\sqrt{2}w+3\text{i})^{2}(\sqrt{2}w-3\text{i})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-75627:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

For the given geometric series, the first term is ${a}_{1}=6.4$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{4.8}{6.4}=0.75.
$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{6.4}{1-0.75} \\  & =\frac{6.4}{0.25} \\  & =25.6.\end{aligned}
$$

q-1092:
The minor of ${b}_{22}=7$ (second row, second column) is the determinant of the remaining entries when the column and row containing $7$ are removed: 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}3 & ∗ & -6 \\ ∗ & 7 & ∗ \\ 5 & ∗ & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

 

So, the minor of ${b}_{22}=7$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 4-(-6)\cdot 5 \\  & =12-(-30) \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
$$

q-69760:
First, we remove the third row and third column:

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}y-x & x & ∗ \\ -x & y+x & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗ & {x}^{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Next, we calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}y-x & x \\ -x & y+x\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}y-x & x \\ -x & y+x\end{aligned}| \\  & =(y-x)\cdot (y+x)-x\cdot (-x) \\  & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} \\  & ={y}^{2}-\cancel{{x}^{2}}+\cancel{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-16423:
**Method 1**

When we multiply a complex number and its conjugate, the result is always the sum of squares of the real part and the imaginary part.

For the given complex number $z=4+9\text{i},$ the real part is $\text{Re}(z)=4,$ and the imaginary part is $\text{Im}(z)=9,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}z\overset{―}{z} & =(\text{Re}(z))^{2}+(\text{Im}(z))^{2} \\  & ={4}^{2}+{9}^{2} \\  & =16+81 \\  & =97.\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

Alternatively, we can actually carry out the process of multiplying the complex number and its conjugate.

To obtain the conjugate of the complex number $z=4+9\text{i},$ we flip the sign of the imaginary part and get $\overset{―}{z}=4-9\text{i}.$

Multiplying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z\overset{―}{z} & =(4+9\text{i})(4-9\text{i}) \\  & ={4}^{2}+(4)(-9)\text{i}+(4)(9)\text{i}-{\text{i}}^{2}(9)^{2} \\  & =16-36\text{i}+36\text{i}-(-1)(81) \\  & =16+81 \\  & =97.\end{aligned}
$$

q-159757:
**Method 1**

When we add a complex number and its conjugate, the result is always twice the real part of the complex number.

For the given complex number $z=-9-\text{i},$ the real part is $Re(z)=-9,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}z+\overset{―}{z} & =2\text{Re}(z) \\  & =2(-9) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

Alternatively, we can actually carry out the process of adding the complex number and its conjugate.

To obtain the conjugate of the complex number $z=-9-\text{i},$ we flip the sign of the imaginary part and get $\overset{―}{z}=-9+\text{i}.$

Adding, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z+\overset{―}{z} & =(-9-\text{i})+(-9+\text{i}) \\  & =(-9+(-9))+\text{i}(-1+1) \\  & =-18+\text{i}\cdot 0 \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

q-2351:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+2t) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-6t+2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-6t+2) \\  & =12t-6\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=2$, we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(2) & =12(2)-6 \\  & =24-6 \\  & =18\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration when $t=2$ seconds is $18\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

q-7186:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\frac{1}{t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-{t}^{-1}) \\  & =1-(-{t}^{-2}) \\  & =1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
